Ball 1 begins in position 1 (ejection chance = 1⁄3).  
Ball 2 begins in position 2 (chance = 5⁄9).  
Ball 3 begins in position 3 (chance = 17⁄27≈0.63).  
Every later ball enters in position 3 only part of the time; its average ejection probability is at most 0.6, never exceeding 17⁄27.  
Thus the highest attainable winning probability is obtained by choosing the unique ball that is certainly in position 3 from the start: ball 3.
Each ball’s fate depends on the platform position in which it first appears.

Ejection chances from a given position:
• Position 1: 1⁄3 (ejected only if piston 1 fires)
• Position 2: 5⁄9 (1⁄3 immediate ejection, or 2⁄3 chance to move to position 1, where it is ejected with probability 1⁄3)
• Position 3: 17⁄27 (1⁄3 immediate ejection, 1⁄3 chance to move to position 2, 1⁄3 chance to move to position 1)

Initial balls
Ball 1 starts in position 1 → 1⁄3 ≈ 0.333
Ball 2 starts in position 2 → 5⁄9 ≈ 0.556
Ball 3 starts in position 3 → 17⁄27 ≈ 0.630

All later balls enter in positions 2 or 3 with long-run weights 0.4 and 0.6, giving an eventual ejection probability of 0.4·5⁄9 + 0.6·17⁄27 = 0.6.  Only Ball 3 exceeds this limit.

Thus the largest winning probability belongs to Ball 3.

All except one form tautologies (are true under every truth assignment). Using implication equivalence (P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q):
1 ¬(A∧B) ↔ (¬A∨¬B)  – De Morgan, tautology.
2 ¬(A∨B) ↔ (¬A∧¬B)  – De Morgan, tautology.
3 (A→B) ↔ (¬B→¬A)   – contraposition, tautology.
4 (A→B) ↔ (¬A∨B)     – definition of →, tautology.
5 (¬A→B) ↔ (A∨¬B)     – but (¬A→B) ≡ A∨B, not A∨¬B, so this biconditional is false when A=F, B=T or A=F, B=F; hence not a tautology.
6 ¬(A→B) ↔ (A∧¬B)    – negated implication, tautology.
Thus #5 is the lone non-equivalent statement.
De Morgan’s laws (1, 2), the contrapositive equivalence (3), the implication definition (4) and the negated-implication rule (6) are all tautologies, hence mutually equivalent.  Statement 5, (¬A → B) ↔ (A ∨ ¬B), is false for A = F,B = T and for A = F,B = F, so it is not a tautology and therefore not equivalent to the others.

Choose guesses g1=g2=g3=x.  Bob is guaranteed x coins iff every legal (a,b,c) has at least one box with ≥x coins.

1.  If x=12
   • Suppose the largest count c were ≤11.  Then all three counts are ≤11, so no pair differs by 6 (maximum difference ≤11−0=11, but to reach 30 one needs ≥12 somewhere).  Hence c must be ≥12 in every legal distribution, so at least one box has ≥12 coins.  With all guesses 12, Bob receives 12 from that box, securing ≥12 coins.

2.  If x=13
   • The distribution (6,12,12) is legal (sum 30 and 12−6=6) and all counts are <13.  Guessing 13 from every box would give Bob 0 coins.  Thus no strategy can guarantee 13 or more.

Therefore the maximum guaranteed number of coins is 12.  Each coin is worth $1,000, so the minimum amount of money Bob can be sure to win is 12×1,000 = 12,000.

2) Some pair differ by exactly 6 ⇒ take x and y with y=x+6 (possible by relabeling).
So the multiset is (x , x+6 , 24−2x).
Because 24−2x≥0 we have 0≤x≤12.
Compute the largest pile for every integer x in that range:
 x=0→max 24
 x=1→max 22
 …
 x=5→max 14
 x=6→max 12
 x=7→max 13
 …
 x=12→max 18
Hence over all legal distributions the largest pile size is always ≥12, while the choice x=6 gives a configuration (6,12,12) whose largest pile is exactly 12. 
Therefore no strategy can guarantee more than 12 coins.
If Bob simply guesses 12 for each box, at least one box must have ≥12 coins, so he is guaranteed to win exactly 12 coins in the worst case.
